bacteriophage: Create one wide, semi-diagrammatic illustration that reads left to right like a story: at the far left, a lone phage is drawn like a tiny lunar lander — an angular protein-shell head packed with a coiled ribbon of genetic instructions, set on a spindly, jointed tail ending in claw-like fibers — latching tail-first onto a much larger rod-shaped bacterium and injecting that ribbon into it like a syringe; next, the same bacterium appears in cutaway, its insides hijacked into an assembly line churning out new phage heads and tails until it bursts open in a starburst of fresh phages that stream toward a second bacterium to repeat the cycle; faint background vignettes of soil, a drop of pond water, and the winding interior of a human gut show phages and bacteria teeming together wherever bacteria live; on the right, a pale human cell sits completely untouched as the swarming phages swerve around it, while beyond it a patient receives an intravenous drip marked with a phage symbol, alongside a cracked, drained antibiotic capsule and a small timeline with a faded map of Eastern Europe hinting at a century of practice; finally, each targeted bacterium is attacked not by one phage but by a cocktail of three or four visibly different species with distinct head shapes and colors, one bacterium raising a shield that deflects a single attacker only to be overwhelmed by the rest, with small arrows and labels throughout keeping every stage readable at a glance.
biosafety-and-biosecurity: A single wide illustration in three connected zones. On the left, inside a transparent-walled containment room, a researcher in a full protective suit carefully handles a glowing sample vial, with small accidental spill droplets hovering mid-air — this half is labeled with a shield marked "BIOSAFETY: accidents." On the right, a heavy steel cabinet with a padlock holds rows of catalogued pathogen vials, while a masked figure in shadow reaches toward it — labeled with a shield marked "BIOSECURITY: theft and misuse." Between and above them sits the visual twist: a computer screen displaying an AI model generating the image of a brand-new virus — a shape that matches nothing in the locked cabinet — its sequence flowing downward as a luminous stream through four successive gates drawn as checkpoints along the chain: a filter over the model's training data, a review committee examining a proposed experiment sheet, a DNA-synthesis company screening an order form, and finally a gloved human hand receiving the sample inside sealed laboratory containment. The composition makes the message legible: the two shields guard against different threats, the novel virus evades the old locked catalogue, and the safeguarded pipeline shows that no designed organism can cause harm without first passing through human hands.
genome-language-model: An illustration showing a long ribbon of DNA unspooling across the page, its familiar double helix dissolving at one end into a stream of the four letters A, T, C, and G, as if the genome were a manuscript being typed. Where the letter stream breaks off mid-sequence, a glowing mechanical pen hovers, with a faint constellation of candidate letters branching from its nib—the model predicting what should come next, some letters bold and others ghosted out. Beside it, a small contrast: a hand with scissors patching a passage of existing text (old-style editing), versus the pen writing a fresh, never-before-seen page. The freshly written sequences fall from the page into a row of tiny laboratory flasks, most of which sit dark and failed, only one or two glowing with life. In the background, a small, simple virus particle is rendered crisp and complete, while a much larger, sprawling cell is sketchy and unfinished, showing the scale of what remains out of reach.
